title: Between Two Languages
author: Barashada Ingiriisiga
description: A reflective journey through the spaces between two languages, where identity bends and blooms in the quiet gaps of daily life.

chapters.title: The Weight of Words
chapters.text:
My mother tongue is a language of warmth and weight. It arrives not as letters on a page but as a physical presence, something you can almost hold in your hands. When I close my eyes and let it rise, I smell my grandmother's kitchen, the slow steam of rice soup simmering on the stove. I hear the creak of the wooden floorboards in the hallway of the house I grew up in, and the low, rumbling laughter of my uncles at a Sunday dinner that never seemed to end. The words themselves have texture. They are round and full, rolled on the back of the tongue, some of them so long that they force you to take a breath before you pronounce them. They demand time. They demand a certain kind of attention, a slowing down.

English, on the other hand, is a different weather system altogether. It is crisp and clean, like the first cool bite of autumn air. It is efficient, almost impatient. Sentences are built to be understood quickly, to move information from one point to another without lingering too long on the feelings in between. I have learned to love its sharpness, its precision, the way a well-placed word can cut through confusion like a blade. But love can be complicated. Sometimes, when I speak English for too long, I feel a strange tightening in my chest, as if my own voice has become a little too small, a little too neat. The words are correct. They land in the right order. But they feel like shoes that fit perfectly but were made for someone else's feet.

I remember the first time I truly understood that I was carrying two different people inside me. It had been raining the whole day, a steady, grey drizzle that turned the pavement to a slick mirror of the city. I was waiting at a bus stop, tired from work, my mind empty and quiet. The glass shelter was streaked with dirt and rainwater, and the city stretched out before me in a blur of lights and moving cars. I was thinking about nothing at all, just watching the water run in small rivers along the curb.

And then, out of nowhere, a phrase surfaced in my mind. It was not in English. It was not a word of my working hours or my quiet apartment. It was a phrase in my mother tongue, something my own grandmother used to say on rainy days like this. She would look out the window at the thick clouds and say, with a sigh, that the sky was "holding its breath." It was a comment meant to capture the heavy, expectant pause before the storm breaks. She was not a poet, my grandmother. She was a practical woman who grew her own vegetables and pressed wrinkles out of shirts by hand. But she understood that the sky could be a living thing, with moods and pauses of its own.

The phrase hung there in my mind, not as a translation, but as a complete feeling. In that single sentence, I was not standing at a bus stop in the late afternoon. I was back in my grandmother's living room, the smell of dust and old wood in the air, the sound of a kettle coming to a boil in the kitchen behind me. I could feel the cool of the tiled floor under my bare feet. I could sense her, standing behind me, placing a hand on my shoulder. The whole memory, so vivid and startling, arrived in the time it takes to blink.

But the bus stop was still there. And the rain was still falling in a straight, grey line. And I was still a person in my work clothes, holding an umbrella I had bought last month from a shop two streets away. In that tiny space of time, I did not belong in either place. I was suspended, caught somewhere between the clatter of an English city and the quiet, deep pull of a home that was thousands of miles away.

That is the feeling I have built my life around. This suspended state, this floating between. People often ask me if I dream in English now. They ask with a sense of curiosity, as if they are asking about a rare animal in a zoo. The truth is impossible to explain simply. It depends on the last time I spoke to my parents, on the films I watch, on the weather. On good days, I dream in a mixture, the words sliding over one another like two different rivers meeting in a wide, calm delta. On other days, I am silent in my dreams, unable to find the correct words, searching for a language that will fully cover the strange, purple feeling of my own inner life.

There is a weight to words that people rarely talk about. When I first arrived here, I was amazed at how light English was, how easily it could be thrown out into the air and caught by others. You could ask a question and get the answer in seconds. You could go to a shop and say, "can I get a coffee, please," and it would be done. The connection. But my mother tongue is heavy. I did not realize this until I started carrying English around with me. Those heavier words, they carry a certain history. They are backed with generations of my family, with the particular story of a country that has seen its own share of rain and silence. When I speak them now, I feel like I am walking with a heavy coat, a weight that keeps me grounded but tiring.

Sometimes, I am afraid of losing the weight. I am afraid that one day I will open my mouth, and the old words will arrive but they will feel empty, hollowed out, like feathers floating after life has left them. At the bus stop, that fear vanished for a second. The sky, the rain, it all belonged to me for that one moment. I was not a person who had left their home; I was a person who carried home within them.

The bus arrived, and the doors opened with a soft hiss. My feet stepped on, my eyes looked at the driver and said, "Thank you," in the sharp, clipped language of this country. The doors closed. I found a seat by the window, and the wet city slid past me. But I was still holding onto the other feeling. I held the weight of that phrase in my pocket, like a stone. And I knew, then, that this was the feeling I would chase for the rest of my life: the impossible alchemy of being two places at once, of speaking two languages, and of understanding that my identity was not a fixed point, but a constant, gentle swaying motion between them.

chapters.title: Translating Home
chapters.text:
My grandmother arrived in March, when the city was still the colour of wet cement. She came with one small suitcase and a canvas bag full of dried herbs, wrapped in newspaper like fish from the market. I met her at the airport and watched her shuffle through the glass doors, a small woman in a black coat, squinting at the arrivals board as if it were a puzzle she had no intention of completing.

She hugged me. The hug was long and wordless, and in that space I smelled her skin, the particular mixture of woodsmoke and rosewater that had scented every room of my childhood. She pulled back and looked at me, then said the phrase I had heard a thousand times before. It was not hello, though that is how the dictionary would translate it. It was not how are you, though a phrasebook might reach for that.

The words meant, roughly, twelve words that I could arrange in English: Did you sleep well, shake off the travel slug, I have been thinking about you since the last time I thought about you, which was my morning coffee and my night washing and every time I noticed a kitchen chair that reminded me of you because you always sat on it the wrong way round. The translation of twelve words is only halfway through, maybe closer to two hundred.

That first night, we sat in my small kitchen and she asked me, in our language, to tell her about my life here. I opened my mouth and met a wall. The story I wanted to tell her required a certain texture, the meaning of a particular word that means both home and the small habits that make a place home, the fold in a blanket, the correct angle of the curtains at noon. English had given me an apartment, a flat with numbered rooms, but the word the word layered, warm, inhabited, complicated, had no English vessel. I told my grandmother I live in a flat and she nodded, but I knew I had given her the skeleton of my life, not its skin.

Later, I tried to explain to her something that had happened at my office that week. A colleague had been sharp with me, and I had stored it in the file of small wrongs. In my mother tongue there was a phrase, a single verb, that meant being quietly and politely wounded, smoothing your face so no one can see you are about to cry. There was also an old word for the warmth of being fed by someone who loves you, which is literally the warmth of the food and the warmth of the person and the warmth of the room combined into one syllable. I tried to explain this to my grandmother in English, and I watched my mouth make a mess of it.

That's, I said, a kind of... a kind of comfort, you know, when someone makes you toast, and it matters because they made it.

She ate her dinner and looked at me with her eyes that had read a thousand more of my silences than my words. Then she laughed a small laugh and said, in our language, I know what you mean. You took the long way round but you still got there. That is what walking is.

Her answer shocked me. All my life I had assumed that the untranslatable was unsaid, a failure of vocabulary. But she was not looking for words. She had been receiving me the whole time with an older instrument, one that reads gesture, silence, the angle of a nervous hand over the coffee cup. For her, the home was not word-for-word. It was feeling-for-feeling.

It was then I began to notice the ways English was not just smaller language, but a differently held house. In her language, you could name several kinds of rain, because the rain was the messenger of the sky and each rain had its own hooded meaning. In English, rain was just rain, a single grey space of sorrow. I had assumed I had lost something irreplaceable. But the truth was quieter and stranger. The thing was not lost; its meaning was renegotiated.

I tried an experiment. The next morning I said to my grandmother, as she put on her coat to go for a walk, good morning, have a good day. The sentence was empty, a functional box. But she turned and said, in the old words, what I meant. She heard my care, she heard my offering, she heard how I was beginning to build a new architecture of love between two languages. She said to me, in recent years, I have learned one sentence in English. She said, is everything well with your heart. She said it slowly, not as an English teacher but as a person learning a secret handshake. I wanted to cry. You do not have to translate home; you have to pack it and let it unfold in the new place, creased but the same cloth.

That week, I took her to a supermarket. She stood in the cereal aisle and picked up boxes, reading labels aloud, she said, they put the word vitality on it, like a medicine. I told her that here, words are in the service of the market, not the soul. She said no, she said it is the same here, only the currency is different. In the old country, the words were heavy with the years of a hundred grandmothers. Here they are light, quick, minted for a fast transaction; but a coin can still buy bread, she said, and a quick word can still carry a small hello if you are brave enough to bend it.

On her last evening, we were sitting at a window with the city spreading out below us like a map of a place I had not yet fully entered. She said, did you know that your grandmother had a word for the afternoon light that comes at the end of autumn when you are going home to a meal? I said I remembered it. She said very, but you do not need the word here. Here you have the sunset, the city lights, the bus route, lifting you forty minutes to a different kind of home. You are not losing the light, you are learning a new way to have the afternoon.

She left the next morning, and the flat felt silent in a familiar way. But from the seat beside me had I noticed she had left one of her scarves by accident, or on purpose. I held it up, smelling for the mixture of woodsmoke and rose, and found it. The word I wanted came to me, first in the old tongue, then in the new. It is the same thing: an afternoon light through a scarf through a day through a life. A home is not a single language, but the intention to build it with whatever words are near.

I sat down at my kitchen table and, for the first time, wrote a letter to my mother in English. I did not try to translate the old words. I wrote new ones, longer ones, made of the grey afternoon and the bus lurch and the small things I now saw as the new constellations. And I understood that what I had lost was not a home, but one way of building it. I was learning to build another. The door was still the door.

chapters.title: The Grammar of Belonging
chapters.text:
The meeting room was a cage of glass and polished wood, and I sat in it, listening to the rhythm of my own voice as it rose and fell in the wrong places. We were discussing the quarterly projections, and I was explaining a discrepancy in the data. My words were accurate, my grammar was correct, and yet, I heard it. The slight flattening of a vowel, the way my 'r' caught at the back of my throat just a little too long. It was a ghost in the machine, a tiny imperfection that no one else seemed to notice, but which for me was a constant, low hum of otherness.

My colleague, David, leaned forward. He had the easy confidence of a man who had never had to think about how he sounded. His sentences were smooth, unbroken stones, polished by a lifetime of use. He interrupted me, not rudely, but with the casual authority of someone who assumes the floor is his by right. "What I think Sarah is trying to say," he began, and then he rephrased my point in his own clean, efficient English. The room nodded. The idea was accepted. It was a small thing, a simple act of translation, but it stung. It was as if my own thought, once it had passed through my mouth, had become something foreign, something that needed to be cleaned up and repackaged before it could be understood.

This is the politics of pronunciation. It is not merely about sounding different; it is about being heard as less. An accent is a biography that you cannot edit. It tells people where you are from, and in doing so, it invites them to make assumptions about where you are going. In the meeting, my accent was a quiet whisper that said, "She is not one of us. She is a visitor, a guest in this language." And a guest, however welcome, is never quite the owner of the house. They are always mindful of the furniture, careful not to break the rules.

Later, in the break room, I stood by the coffee machine, trying to make small talk with a woman from marketing. She was telling a story about her weekend, and I laughed at the right moments, my smile fixed in place. I found myself mirroring her intonation, flattening my vowels just a little more, softening my consonants. It was an unconscious act, this code-switching, but it was also a betrayal. I was editing myself, removing the rough edges of my identity to make myself smoother, more palatable. The words felt like borrowed clothes, slightly too tight in the shoulders but acceptable for a short outing. Each time I did this, I felt a small piece of my mother tongue recede further into the shadows, waiting for me to return.

Then came the comment. It was from Peter, a senior manager, who had just returned from a conference in my home country. He was being friendly, I knew, but his words landed with an unexpected weight. "You know, I never would have guessed you were from there," he said, swirling his tea. "Your English is so... complete. You've really lost most of it."

Lost most of it. He meant the accent, of course. He was offering me a compliment, a certificate of assimilation. But the phrase burrowed into me. What exactly had I lost? I had lost the soft, melodic rise and fall of my first language. I had lost the ability to say certain phrases without a pang of distance. I had lost the warmth that seemed to live in the very syllables of my childhood tongue, a warmth that felt impossible to replicate in this new, efficient language. English was a language of precision, of clear lines and defined edges. It was excellent for contracts, for instructions, for expressing a sharp, analytical thought. But it often felt like a house with the heating off.

Peter's comment forced a question to the surface, a question I had been avoiding for years. Who am I when I speak the new language fluently, but without inherited warmth? When I can argue a point in a boardroom with perfect clarity, but I cannot find the words to comfort a friend in the way my grandmother would have? The fluency I had worked so hard to achieve felt, in that moment, like a magnificent, hollow structure. I had built it brick by brick, word by word, but I had not been able to install the central heating. The emotional resonance, the deep, instinctive connection to the sounds themselves, remained locked in a different part of my brain, in a different house.

I thought of my mother tongue, with its words that could bend and stretch to hold a hug, a scolding, and a shared joke all at once. English, for all its richness, seemed to demand a certain emotional hygiene. It kept things tidy. You were "fine," not "full of a quiet, humming ache." You were "busy," not "torn into a thousand small pieces by the day." To speak it well was to agree to its terms, to accept its emotional grammar.

In that moment, standing by the coffee machine, I felt the space between my two selves stretch wide. One self was here, in this bright, clean room, speaking the language of success and productivity. The other self was elsewhere, in a kitchen that smelled of spices and old wood, speaking a language that felt like a heartbeat. Peter saw only the first self. My colleague David heard only the first self. But I could feel the second one, silent and watchful, a permanent resident in the house of my mind.

Perhaps belonging is not a place you arrive at, but a grammar you learn. And perhaps I am forever bilingual in the grammar of belonging itself-fluent in the rules of one world, and native to the soul of another. The question Peter asked with his compliment was not about my accent at all. It was about which grammar I would choose to live by. And as I walked back to my desk, I realised I did not have an answer. I only had the feeling of being a translation, a version of myself that was accurate, but never quite the original.

chapters.title: Lullabies in a Borrowed Tongue
chapters.text:
The first time I held my daughter, she was impossibly small, a warm weight against my chest whose entire world existed in the space between my arms and the steady rhythm of my breathing. In those first few hours, I did not think about language at all. We communicated in the old way, before words, through touch and the particular sound of a heartbeat that had been her home for nine months. And then, somewhere between the second and third night, she began to cry, a thin, furious sound that demanded something I could not yet name. I held her close and, without thinking, I began to sing.

It was a lullaby I had grown up with, a simple tune about the moon hiding behind a mountain, told in the soft vowels of my mother tongue. The words came, but they came slowly, shaped by years of disuse. They felt heavy on my tongue, like objects I had once known intimately but could no longer lift with ease. I stumbled on a phrase, hesitated, and the song broke apart. My daughter quieted for a moment, as if confused, and then cried again with renewed urgency.

I switched to English. Hush, little baby, the lyrics promised a gift of something ordinary, a diamond ring that would never shine. I was easier in that language, smoother, sharper. The words slid out without effort, and I felt in that a strange shame. Here I was, a parent, failing to give my child the warmth that had carried me like a river as a mother. What she would receive instead was a borrowed warm river, one I had traveled to, but never quite dived into.

That night, after my daughter had finally drifted off, I sat in a dark room, the city lit outside the window, and I counted my losses like beads on a chain. I would never, I realized, whisper to her the words that had passed between my mothers mother and her mother before her. Our jokes would not land the same way in this new language. The stories I told her of my childhood would be translated, turned into watercolors of a place I could no longer fully visit. I felt like a messenger who had been handed a gift he was bound to carry, but was forbidden to open for himself.

And yet, in the weeks that followed, I saw something strange happen. When my daughter was tired, my hands would reach for my phone to play a sound, anything to calm. But my heart would push my mouth to hum that old melody, the one that had tripped my tongue. I began to practice it alone, in the kitchen while a threat was boiling, or in the whipping the shower. I guessed letters, looked words up, and rebuilt the sounds of my childhood like a craftsperson staring at a broken cup. There was shame in this confession to the generation, but two made way for his, and slowness became a kind of care.

One evening when she must have been almost six months old, I walked into her room to find her nearly asleep. Her eyes were fluttering, and she looked breathless. I began the lullaby in my mother tongue. This time, the words did not trip. They found familiar paths, and the melody settled into me like a hand fitted into a glove. Her breathing slowed, deepened. When I reached the second verse, I sang it in English, first out of a habit, but also out of a strange sense of honesty. Her face, relaxed, made no sign of noticing. The melody, held both sets of words together, the old and the borrowed, as if the two languages were simply two dresses a single heart wore.

In that moment, I saw something clear. I was not giving my daughter a pure inheritance-a single language, a single melody, a single home. I was giving her a mosaic. Not the kind that is painted to look whole, but the kind in which each piece is visible, and the gaps between them are part of the design. She would grow up with certain silences, difficulties about words my parents know and I no longer do. But she would also grow up with the everyday of two tongues in her mouth, of being able to say goodnight in two sounds, of hearing the echo of a mountain in her mother's English.

I thought about my own parents, and the shame I sometimes carried for leaving them behind in a language. I understood then that the act of losing a language is not always a clean hand over. My mother tongue had not vanished; it had been sheet of paper folded into my new life. It surfaced when I was tired, when I was afraid, when I held my child close. It simply lived now, in a different shape, like a river that moves because it must.

When my daughter learned her first words, she said them in English. When she learned to whisper her own song, it was a mishmash of English and my careful, practiced phrases. She invented words of her own, and I knew those too would bloom and be lost. I sang to her, sometimes in English, sometimes in the old language, and I no longer felt the sting of it. The way I sang was not a loss, but a fusion.

One evening, unlike now grown, she was nine months old, and we sat by the window in the last light of the day. She reached up and touched my mouth, her fingers light and curious, almost as if to understand the sound. I sang the old lullaby, and she hummed along, a hollow of high, wooden notes without words. I realized then that I did not need to hand her the map to a land I had left. I only needed to give her the song, and she would find her own way to the mountain, the moon, and her own language of belonging. The music, I understood, does not belong to one or the other to the river that runs between them.

chapters.title: The Space Between
chapters.text:
There is a bridge I cross most mornings, a wide stone arch that spans the grey river dividing the old city from the new. I have crossed it hundreds of times, usually with my mind fixed on the day ahead, my feet moving without instruction. But this morning, I stopped. I stood in the middle of the span, my hands resting on the cold stone, and I watched the water move beneath me. The river did not ask where it came from or where it was going; it simply carried both the memory of the mountains and the promise of the sea in the same current.

I thought about how I had come to this city, and how this city had come to me. For years, I had treated the space between my two languages as a kind of no-man's land, a territory I had to cross quickly to avoid being caught in the open. When I spoke English, I felt I was wearing a suit that did not quite fit, the sleeves a little too long, the collar a little too stiff. When I spoke my mother tongue, I felt the sharp ache of distance, the knowledge that the people I loved were far away, and that the language itself had begun to change without me. I was always leaving one shore to reach the other, never quite standing still.

But standing on the bridge, I began to see it differently. The space between was not empty. It was full of movement, full of traffic. There were words that travelled from one side to the other, carrying small gifts of meaning. There were silences that hung in the air like mist, waiting to be interpreted. I listened to the two voices inside me, and for the first time, I did not try to choose between them. I let them speak at once, a kind of duet that I had never allowed myself to hear.

The voice of my mother tongue was low and warm, like the smell of bread in a kitchen I had known as a child. It had the rhythm of my grandmother's hands, the way she would pat the dough and hum a tune that had no name. This voice did not hurry. It took its time, circling a feeling until it found the right word, and if the word did not exist, it invented one, or it used a gesture, or it simply laughed. It was a language of the body as much as the mouth, a language that assumed you had all the time in the world to say what you meant.

The voice of English was different. It was clear and bright, like the light on the river this morning. It cut through fog, named things precisely, and moved at the speed of the city around me. This voice had given me a kind of freedom, a passport to conversations I could not have had in my old life. It had taught me to be direct, to say what I needed, to ask for what I wanted. In English, I had learned to be an adult in a new way, to negotiate, to advocate, to stand up straight and make my point.

For a long time, I had thought these two voices were enemies, competing for the same small space inside me. But on the bridge, I understood that they were not rivals. They were two instruments in the same orchestra, playing different parts of the same score. The warmth of one did not cancel the precision of the other. The slowness of one did not make the speed of the other shallow. They were both mine, and they were both true.

I thought about my child, who was learning to sing in both languages, who would grow up with a different kind of bridge inside them. I did not know yet what they would lose or gain, what words would feel like home and what words would feel like borrowed clothes. But I hoped they would learn what I was learning now: that to live between languages is not to live in a smaller world, but in a wider one. It is to see that every word has a shadow, every phrase a second meaning, every silence a story.

This is the work of translation, I realised. Not the mechanical act of swapping one word for another, but the deeper act of carrying meaning across the current, of finding the shape of a thought in a new body. Every time I speak, I am translating myself. I am taking the person I was in my mother tongue and introducing them to the person I am becoming in English. Sometimes they argue. Sometimes they misunderstand each other. But more and more, they are learning to listen.

I thought of the people I had met in this city, the friends who had never heard my first language, who knew me only through the clear, bright voice of English. They did not know the warmth of my grandmother's kitchen, the weight of certain words that could hold an entire childhood. But they knew me. They knew the person I had chosen to become, the one who could say what she meant and ask for what she needed. And I thought of the people I had left behind, who heard the old voice when I called, who could tell from a single syllable that I had changed, that I was carrying a new kind of light.

The bridge was not a place of lack. It was a place of meeting. It was where the river of my past flowed into the sea of my present, and the water did not ask which current was more important. It simply carried both, and in the carrying, it became something deeper, something wider.

I lifted my hands from the stone and began to walk again. The city was waking up around me, the traffic beginning to hum, the shops opening their doors. I did not feel divided. I felt multiplied. The two voices inside me were not fighting for space; they were making room for each other, building a home that had many rooms, many windows, many doors.

I am not one language or the other, I thought. I am the space between, and the space between is not empty. It is full of everything I have ever been and everything I am still becoming.
